name: Kairouan
info: Kairouan is a city in central Tunisia, founded by the Umayyads around 670 as a military post for the conquest of the West, and later the capital of the Aghlabids and the Zirids and a centre of Islamic learning.

facts.founded: Around 670, when the Arab general Uqba ibn Nafi, acting for Caliph Mu'awiya, chose the site for a military post; a Byzantine garrison town, Kamounia, had stood there before the Arab conquest.
facts.where: On a plain inland in central Tunisia, 50 km from the east coast, west of Sousse and 184 km from Tunis.
facts.known: A military foundation of the Arab conquest; capital of the Aghlabids; the Great Mosque and its teaching; Maliki scholarship; a Jewish centre of Talmudic learning; the Aghlabid basins; destruction by the Banu Hilal in 1057
facts.today: Kairouan is the capital of the Kairouan Governorate in Tunisia, and its old city is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

t: Kairouan was founded around 670 as an Arab military post far from the sea, and under the Aghlabids (800 to 909) it became a capital and a centre of Islamic and secular learning.
The Fatimids neglected it after 909 and the Zirids ruled again from it, until the Banu Hilal and Banu Sulaym took it in 1057 and ended its standing as the leading city of Ifriqiya.
The city began to recover under the Hafsids in the 13th century, was taken by the French in 1881, and kept its Great Mosque, its basins and its place in Islamic tradition.
dyk: Local tradition holds that seven pilgrimages to the Great Mosque of Kairouan equal one pilgrimage to Mecca, and according to some this makes it the fourth holiest city in Islam.
ev: Uqba ibn Nafi chooses the site of Kairouan for a military post
The Berber leader Al-Kahina is killed and her army defeated
Handhala ibn Safwan defeats the great Berber army near the city
Ibrahim ibn al-Aghlab becomes emir of Ifriqiya and makes Kairouan his capital
The Fatimids overthrow the Aghlabids and neglect Kairouan
The Banu Hilal take Kairouan from the Zirids and destroy it
Under the Hafsids the city begins to emerge from its ruins
The French take Kairouan and open it to non-Muslims

sections.origins:
Kairouan was founded around 670, when the Arab general Uqba ibn Nafi, acting for Caliph Mu'awiya, selected a site in the middle of a dense forest, then infested with wild beasts and reptiles, for a military post from which to conquer the West. A town called Kamounia had stood where Kairouan now stands, and it had housed a Byzantine garrison before the Arab conquest. The site lay far from the sea, and so was safe from the attacks of the Berbers, who had fiercely resisted the Arab invasion.

The name is the Arabic al-Qayrawan, meaning a military group or a caravan, borrowed early from the Middle Persian word karawan, which meant a military column or a caravan. In Berber the city was once called Tikirwan, thought to be an adaptation of the Arabic name. Early modern English sometimes wrote it Cairoan. The Great Mosque, the city's main landmark, was originally built when Kairouan was founded.

Berber resistance continued after the founding. Kusaila led it first, and his troops killed Uqba at Biskra about fifteen years after the military post was established. A Berber woman called Al-Kahina then led it, until she was killed and her army defeated in 702. A mass conversion of the Berbers to Islam followed.
sections.growth:
By 745 Kairouan was already a developed city with luxuriant gardens and olive groves. Its first great period began in 800, when Caliph Harun ar-Rashid in Baghdad confirmed Ibrahim ibn al-Aghlab as emir and hereditary ruler of Ifriqiya. The Aghlabid emirs ruled between 800 and 909, embellished Kairouan and made it their capital. It became famous for its wealth and prosperity, reaching the levels of Basra and Kufa.

The Aghlabids rebuilt the great mosque and established in it a university, a centre of education in Islamic thought and in the secular sciences, with a role comparable to that of the University of Paris in the Middle Ages. In the 9th century scholars came from across the Islamic world, and Imam Sahnun and Asad ibn al-Furat made the city a centre for spreading the Islamic sciences. The Aghlabids also built palaces, fortifications and waterworks, of which only the pools remain, and they conquered Sicily in 827.

After the Fatimids had moved on to Egypt and left the Zirids as their vassals in Ifriqiya, the Zirids governed again from Kairouan. Schools and universities flourished, overseas trade in local manufactures and farm produce ran high, and the courts of the Zirid rulers were centres of refinement.
sections.rulers:
Kairouan began as a post of the Umayyad caliphs, whose general Uqba ibn Nafi founded it. In October 741, during the Great Berber Revolt, the Ifriqiyan army and a Syrian force sent by the caliph were destroyed by the Berbers at the Battle of Bagdoura. The Umayyad Caliph Hisham then appointed Handhala ibn Safwan governor of Ifriqiya, and he reached Kairouan around April 742. In 745 Kharijite Berbers captured the city, and power struggles continued until Ibrahim ibn al-Aghlab recaptured it at the end of the 8th century.

The Aghlabid dynasty, which Ibrahim founded, ruled Ifriqiya between 800 and 909 with Kairouan as its capital. In 893 the Kutama Berbers began the movement of the Shiite Fatimids through the mission of Abdullah al Mahdi, and in 909 the Fatimids overthrew the Sunni Aghlabids. They lived first at Raqqada and soon moved their capital to the newly built Al Mahdiyah on the east coast. They later moved east to found Cairo, leaving the Zirids as their vassals in Ifriqiya.

The Zirids declared their independence from Cairo and their conversion to Sunni Islam in 1045, by giving allegiance to Baghdad. The Hafsids ruled Ifriqiya in the 13th century, and the Husainid dynasty later. The French took Kairouan in 1881.
sections.life:
In the 9th to 11th centuries Kairouan was one of the great centres of Islamic civilisation, with a reputation as a hotbed of scholarship across the Maghreb. The Great Mosque was both a place of prayer and a centre for teaching the Islamic sciences under the Maliki current. A tradition particular to Kairouan used Islamic law to enforce monogamy, by stipulating it in the marriage contract. Sufi festivals are held in the city in memory of saints.

Jews were among the original settlers of Kairouan. Their community's golden era began in the late 8th century and lasted until the early 11th century, and for at least three generations it was a world centre of Talmudic and Halakhic scholarship. A Christian community existed during the early 11th century. Before the French arrived in 1881, non-Muslims were forbidden to live in the city.

Al-Idrisi, writing in the 12th century, recorded that Kairouan was originally two cities, Kairouan itself and Sabra, which was the royal residence and at the height of its prosperity contained three hundred baths. He wrote that the city's water supply was scarce and that its people drank from a great cistern within the city. The Aghlabid basins of the 9th century, outside the ramparts, held a total of 68,800 cubic metres of water.
sections.crises:
Kairouan was repeatedly threatened during the Berber revolts. After the defeat at Bagdoura in 741, the whole of Ifriqiya lay open to the rebels. In 742 the qadi Abd al-Rahman ibn Oqba al-Ghaffari defended the city against an attack by the Sufrite leader Oqasha ibn Ayub al-Fezari. Handhala ibn Safwan then defeated Oqasha at El-Qarn and is said to have put the entire population of Kairouan under arms to face a second Berber army said to number some 300,000.

In perhaps the bloodiest encounter of the Berber wars, Handhala defeated that army at al-Asnam in May 742, perhaps a little later, three miles outside the city. Some 120,000 to 180,000 Berbers, including their commander Abd al-Wahid ibn Yazid, fell in that single battle. Kharijite Berbers captured the city in 745.

The worst blow came after the Zirids broke with Cairo in 1045. As punishment the Fatimid Caliph al-Mustansir Billah sent the Arab tribes of the Banu Hilal and Banu Sulaym to invade Ifriqiya. They took Kairouan from the Zirids in 1057 and destroyed it, so that it never regained its former importance. Their influx was a major factor in the spread of nomadism where agriculture had been dominant, and in most of the country the land was laid waste for nearly two centuries. Al-Idrisi described the city in the 12th century as largely in ruins, with only a portion of it enclosed by an earthen wall.
sections.legacy:
The Great Mosque of Sidi-Uqba, also called the Great Mosque of Kairouan, is one of the largest Islamic monuments in North Africa and one of the oldest places of worship in the Islamic world. It was rebuilt substantially under the Aghlabids in the 9th century and now occupies over 9,000 square metres. The Mosque of the Three Doors was founded in 866, and its facade carries three inscriptions in Kufic script. The Zawiya of Sidi Sahib, or Mosque of the Barber, holds the tomb of Abu Zama' al-Balawi, who according to legend kept three hairs of Muhammad's beard.

The Aghlabid basins are considered to be among the most important hydraulic systems in the history of the Muslim world. The French built the Sousse to Kairouan railway, which ran from 1882 to 1996. The old city and its monuments became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1988.

Kairouan is today the capital of the Kairouan Governorate in Tunisia, and in 2014 it had about 187,000 inhabitants. The Jewish community returned only after Tunisia became a French protectorate in 1881 and had disappeared by the 1960s; its dilapidated cemetery remains. The city is also known for its pastries, such as zlebia and makroudh.

summary: Kairouan, in central Tunisia, was founded around 670 as an Arab military post. It was the Aghlabid capital and a centre of Islamic and Jewish learning until the Banu Hilal destroyed it in 1057, and its Great Mosque still stands.
notes: Only one article was available; no history article exists, so nothing was cross-checked.
START: article says foundation 'about the year 670' (the lead says 'around 670'); circa true.
Berber chronology: Uqba killed by Kusaila 'about fifteen years after' the founding; Al-Kahina's death 702. No date given for Kusaila's death.

Handhala's battle: the article says 'perhaps a little later' than May 742 and gives 120,000-180,000 dead and 'said to be some 300,000'; kept with the hedges. The 'put the entire population under arms' is 'is said to have'; I wrote 'is said to have'.
Aghlabid dates: 800-909; Ibrahim recaptured Kairouan 'at the end of the 8th century'. The Aghlabids' conquest of Sicily 827 is given.

The article's Aghlabid passage includes charges of drunkenness and crippling taxation from Charlemagne's envoys; left out as tendentious. 'Brilliant focus', 'temple of knowledge', 'magnificent' also left out as praise.

The article compares the university's role to the University of Paris; I attributed the comparison to the article ('whose role the article compares'), which speaks of the source: now reworded as comparable to the University of Paris.
Zirid return: the article does not date the Zirids' rule from Kairouan except 1045 (independence) and 1057 (loss); 'ruled again from Kairouan' kept undated.

Fatimid text: 'Husainid dynasty' and Hafsids are given without dates beyond 'in the 13th century' for the Hafsids; the Husainid line is only said to have given the city an honorable place. I did not say more.
Event '13th century' label: the article says that under the Hafsids 'the city started to emerge from its ruins'.
Al-Idrisi's text gives the cistern as square, 200 cubits a side; I left the dimensions out. His claims are the 12th-century account and flagged as his.
The legend of Abu Zama' al-Balawi and the pilgrimage equivalence are attributed to legend and local tradition. No depiction of Muhammad is described.
Left out as tourism, economy, climate, film or notable-people material per the guide; Su'da, Fatima al-Fihriya and modern figures omitted. The December 2023 wall collapse omitted.

The article gives 'Between the 9th and 11th centuries AD' for the city's scholarly peak; the Jewish golden era 'late 8th century to early 11th century'. The article says the Jewish community was a world centre 'for at least three generations'.
The article's text 'Some 1,700 years of intermittent but continual progress was undone within a decade' contradicts the city's founding in 670 (it refers to the country); left out.
